scene.testo: Albert Kesselring called him cautious. That was the word. When Allied officers asked Hitler's commander in Italy about Field Marshal Montgomery, he gave the verdict his old rival Rommel had written down first. What he left out was far darker.

Spring 1945. The war in Europe is over. In an Allied interrogation, German generals are asked about their enemies. One question comes about Montgomery. The answer sounds like praise. But who is really speaking, Kesselring or a dead man?
The real story is not the compliment. It is the one word Kesselring chose, where it came from, and why it explains how Montgomery beat the Germans from the desert of Egypt to the mountains of Italy.
First, the man being questioned. Albert Kesselring was a field marshal of the Luftwaffe who ended the war as Commander in Chief West. American troops captured him in Austria on May 6, 1945.
Allied reporters knew him as Smiling Albert. The nickname came from his cheerful public face. Behind it stood a commander who had fought British forces in the Mediterranean for more than three years.

He was not a daring raider like Rommel. He started as an artillery officer, then moved to the air force. He knew supply lines, airfields and ports, the plain arithmetic of war. That arithmetic matters later.

In December 1941, Hitler sent him south as Commander in Chief South. His job: control the air and sea routes across the Mediterranean so supplies could reach Rommel's army in North Africa. Malta kept sinking his ships.

That put Kesselring and Rommel in a strange partnership. Kesselring was the senior officer on paper. In practice, Rommel often went his own way. The two men argued over supplies and strategy. Both would meet the same enemy.

In August 1942, a new British commander arrived in the desert: Lieutenant General Bernard Montgomery. He took over the British Eighth Army, which had just retreated deep into Egypt. He ordered that there would be no further retreat.

Rommel struck first, at Alam Halfa, in early September. Montgomery did not chase him. He held his ground, let the attack fail, and kept his army intact. It was no accident. Rommel later wrote about that patience.

Then came October 23, 1942, El Alamein. More than 800 British guns opened fire in the dark. Rommel was not there. He was in Austria on sick leave. His deputy, General Stumme, died of a heart attack on the second day.

Rommel flew back and found his army in a vise. The British were grinding forward in a slow, planned battle, twelve days of it. They had far more tanks, more guns, more fuel. Rommel's fuel was nearly gone.

On November 3, Hitler ordered Rommel to hold the line, victory or death. Rommel hesitated, then ordered the retreat anyway. His army began a march of more than 1,000 miles west. Remember this retreat.

Rommel's private papers, published after the war, describe a British pursuit that was cautious and methodical. Montgomery gathered strength before every step and would not gamble. That slowness let much of Rommel's army escape. Hold on to the word cautious.
Kesselring watched from Rome. Days after Alamein, Allied forces landed in Algeria and Morocco. Kesselring rushed German troops into Tunisia by air and sea. He held the door open for six more months.

The African campaign ended in May 1943. Roughly 250,000 Axis soldiers surrendered in Tunisia. Rommel had left Africa in March, sick and out of favor. Kesselring now had to defend Italy itself. Montgomery would be waiting there too.

July 1943: the Allies invaded Sicily. Montgomery led the British Eighth Army up the island's east coast. Kesselring's forces fought a delaying battle, then ferried tens of thousands of troops across the Strait of Messina to the mainland.

September 3, 1943: Montgomery crossed into the toe of Italy. Kesselring did not try to stop him on the beaches. He chose the mountains and rivers, where small German units could hold up much larger forces.

Why does this matter for the question? Because in Italy, Kesselring studied Montgomery up close. Not as a rumor, but as a rival whose every move he had to counter. And what he saw matched Rommel's verdict.

Montgomery never hid it. His method was to prepare carefully, build overwhelming strength, and open with a massive artillery barrage. He wanted to avoid any defeat he could prevent. Allied generals were divided over whether this was wisdom or timidity.

Montgomery left Italy at the end of 1943 to prepare for Normandy. Kesselring stayed. He held the Gustav Line through the winter, including Monte Cassino, and Rome did not fall until June 4, 1944. Slow, costly, methodical.

Now return to the room. In the weeks after his capture, Kesselring sat before Allied interrogators. He was a prisoner with a reputation to protect. They wanted to know how the Germans judged their enemy.

The question was simple: what did he think of Montgomery? Kesselring's answer, recorded in his postwar statements and memoirs, began with respect. Montgomery was thorough. Montgomery was methodical. Then came the word, and it was not his own.

Cautious. That was the answer. Kesselring's verdict echoed what Rommel had written: Montgomery was careful, deliberate, and unwilling to gamble. It was a dead man's judgment, repeated by the officer who had often argued with him.

The word cut two ways. It was a compliment, because a cautious commander does not waste soldiers. His men trusted him for that. It was also a criticism, because caution gave the Germans time. Time was what Kesselring needed.
Time is what Rommel got after Alamein. Time is what Kesselring got in Sicily and along the Gustav Line. Each delay cost the Allies weeks or months. Each month meant more dead on both sides.

But here is the part Kesselring did not say. Praise for a rival can double as an excuse. If the enemy is a master of method, then losing to him is no disgrace. It runs through many postwar German memoirs.

There was something else in his record. In March 1944, after a bomb killed German policemen in Rome, 335 Italians were shot in the Ardeatine Caves. Kesselring was the commander in charge of the region.

A British military court in Venice convicted him in 1947 over the Ardeatine killings and anti-partisan reprisals. It sentenced him to death. The sentence was commuted to life, and he was released in 1952. British judges decided his fate.

Nuremberg gave German officers a public stage, and Kesselring used it. In March 1946, he appeared as a witness for Hermann Göring and defended the Luftwaffe's record. He spoke as a professional soldier.

Why does one word from an interrogation matter? Because it shows how the German high command judged its enemy. They did not fear Montgomery as a lightning raider. They respected him as a system. A system that ground forward and rarely broke.

Montgomery himself would not have denied it. At Alamein, he announced his plan in advance and followed it. The Eighth Army lost about 13,500 men in twelve days. Historians still debate whether it could have been won faster.

The consequence is simple. Caution made Montgomery hard to beat. It also made him slow to finish a beaten enemy. Rommel's army escaped to Tunisia, and Kesselring's forces escaped Sicily. Both enemies lived to fight again.

Italy shows the cost. The Allies landed on the mainland in September 1943. German forces in Italy did not surrender until May 2, 1945, nearly twenty months later. Mountains helped Kesselring. So did patient opponents.

Rommel believed material decided Alamein. He wrote that an army without fuel and ammunition cannot fight well. Kesselring knew that problem better than anyone, because he had run the supply line. Their conclusion was shared.

Kesselring died in 1960. The Allied files keep the answer: a compliment, an echo, and a silence. Rommel wrote the word. Kesselring repeated it. Subscribe for more of what the men on the other side said in their own words.

descrizione:
They asked Kesselring about Montgomery. He repeated what Rommel said. In Allied interrogation after his capture in 1945, Hitler's field marshal in Italy was asked to judge his British rival, and he gave one word that Rommel had written first.

From El Alamein and Tunisia to Sicily, Monte Cassino and the Gustav Line, this documentary follows the German generals interrogated by the Allies, the Afrika Korps, the Nuremberg trials and the war crimes trial in Venice. It shows why the verdict mattered and what Kesselring left out.

Based on interrogation reports, memoirs and trial records. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more German generals in their own words.
